title: Millbind
concept: One crank is fixed on the yard for the whole game — it never relocates — and every round it turns the whole machine once. Because meshed gears turn opposite ways, a millstone grinds only when an ODD number of gears stands between it and the crank, and the longer that running chain is, the more it grinds: one pellet per gear of the drive. So the game's two fights fall out of one fact of engineering. Everyone wants a long, odd, clockwise chain into their own millstone; everyone else wants to drop one gear into that chain and flip it dead, or steal the scarce full-height tandems that are the only bridges between the tall and low tooth tiers. And the whole race is against a shared granary that drains every grind: when it runs dry the milling stops for good. A turn is choosing whether to lengthen your own machine, bridge a tier, or sabotage a neighbour's, then watching the crank turn and counting your grist.
novelty: Scoring is continuous in the distance a millstone stands from a FIXED, never-relocated crank: a mill grinds one pellet for every gear in the shortest running chain back to the crank, but only if that count is odd (clockwise). This inverts the mechanism the pipeline's previous gate killed — the old joke was that the free-relocating crank made a long chain worthless; now the crank cannot move, so distance to it is the whole pay-off, and a long chain is the point rather than the trap. Two fights fall out of that one fact. A mill owner wants a long clockwise drive; every other player wants to insert a single gear into that drive, which flips the chain's parity and deadens the millstone, and the scarce full-height tandems are the only supply pieces that weld the two tooth tiers so a drive can be bridged at all. The race is a shared, finite granary that drains each grind and ends the game, so passing can never reach the end and stalling simply concedes the granary. The prior-art confirmation for the underlying meshing-parity/bind base was run when the game was first proposed (closest shipped: Fifth Gear, a colour-ownership connection race with no rotation direction and a static central white gear; Gearworks, card iconography; Gearplexed, a video-game puzzle). An attempted re-run of the confirmation queries for the reworked mechanism through WebSearch returned a hard API error in this environment, so this rework stands on the original vetted base rather than on a fresh pass; flag for a one-query re-run by the next agent with working search before shipping.

art_direction.form_language: Cast-iron mill gearing on a plank floor: heavy chamfered gear rims, thick spoked webs with big round lightening holes, nothing thinner than a finger. The board is a slab of milled floor with raised plank ribs and a chamfered skirt, bristling with stubby pins. Everything reads as machined and greased, not printed — no filigree, no lattice, no decorative spindles.
art_direction.silhouette: A hexagonal mill floor sprouting a forest of cogs at two clearly different heights, a single fixed crank standing among them always in the same place round after round, and four furrowed millstones tethered to it by chains of toothed wheels — an ironworks seen from the gantry, several days into a long grind.
art_direction.part_vocabulary: gear_low is a squat toothed puck whose teeth start at the floor — teeth DOWN; gear_high is the same tooth ring carried at the top of a plain smooth column, so it reads as a lamppost with teeth UP in the air and a bare shaft below; gear_tandem is a full barrel of teeth from floor to pin top, the tallest toothed thing on the board and obviously the piece that can touch both heights and is therefore the scarce bridge every long drive needs; mill_gear is a full-height gear crowned by a dressed grinding disc cut with radial furrows, topped by a prism hub with three, four, five or six sides — the hub prism is a player's identity for the whole game and is read by counting flats, never by colour; crank_gear is the only piece with an arm and a knurled knob and the only one bearing a direction arrow, and because it stays in one place for the whole game the table reads it as the still heart of the machine; grain_pellet is a small smooth domed washer with no teeth at all, so a score piece can never be mistaken for a game piece.
art_direction.surface_treatment: 1.2mm-deep radial furrow dressing (the harp pattern of a real millstone) across every mill_gear crown; 1.2mm raised sills ring the eighteen outer pins to mark yard positions where a millstone or the fixed crank may stand; 1mm raised plank ribs run across the board floor between pins so the yard reads as a floor rather than a jig plate; 1.2mm raised arrow and knurl on the crank cap; 1mm chevron water-texture on each sack_spindle base and on the granary_bin's front.
art_direction.hero_shot: Straight-down overhead just after a grind: one fixed crank at the rim, a long low chain running from it across the yard and up through a single full-height tandem into a stand of tall high-tier wheels, one millstone mid-drive with its furrows catching the light and a dead counterclockwise neighbour standing silent, and four spindles of stacked grain washers at visibly different heights telling the whole race at a glance.

components.name: yard_board
components.desc: Hexagonal slab, ~230mm corner to corner, ~12mm thick with a chamfered skirt. 37 integral pins (8mm diameter, 30mm tall, generous 0.5mm running clearance to gear bores) on a triangular lattice at 30mm spacing — centre, ring of 6, ring of 12, ring of 18. The 18 outer-ring pins each sit inside a 1.2mm raised sill marking them as yard positions, the only pins a mill_gear or the crank_gear may stand on. Floor between pins carries 1mm raised plank ribs. Fits the P2S bed in one piece.

components.name: gear_low
components.desc: Low-tier gear: 12 teeth on a 30mm pitch circle (~35mm outside diameter), teeth band occupying the LOWER half of the pin height starting just above the floor, ~10mm face. 8.6mm bore, three round lightening holes in the web for grip, chamfered tooth crowns and generous backlash so a long train turns freely by hand. Meshes only with another gear_low, or with a full-height piece, on a neighbouring pin.

components.name: gear_high
components.desc: High-tier gear: the same 12-tooth, 30mm-pitch ring, but carried at the TOP of a plain smooth column so the teeth occupy the UPPER half of the pin height and nothing but bare shaft sits below. Same bore and clearance. Meshes only with another gear_high, or with a full-height piece.

components.name: gear_tandem
components.desc: Full-height gear: the same tooth profile run the whole pin height as one barrel of teeth, ~28mm face. The only supply piece that meshes with both tiers, and therefore the scarce bridge every drive needs to cross from the low half of the yard to the high half. There are only three in the box and everyone wants them.

components.name: mill_gear_tri
components.desc: Millstone, three-sided hub. Full-height tooth barrel like gear_tandem, crowned by a dressed grinding disc cut with 1.2mm radial furrows; the crown does not overhang the tooth circle, so it never fouls a neighbouring pin. A triangular prism hub rises from the crown as a finger grip and as its owner's mark.

components.name: mill_gear_square
components.desc: Millstone, four-sided hub. Identical to mill_gear_tri apart from the square prism hub.

components.name: mill_gear_penta
components.desc: Millstone, five-sided hub. Identical to mill_gear_tri apart from the pentagonal prism hub.

components.name: mill_gear_hex
components.desc: Millstone, six-sided hub. Identical to mill_gear_tri apart from the hexagonal prism hub.

components.name: crank_gear
components.desc: The only power in the box, and it never moves: a full-height tooth barrel with a solid cap carrying an offset arm and a 14mm knurled knob standing 22mm proud, plus a 1.2mm raised arrow showing the clockwise driving direction. Stood once at setup on a yard pin and left there for the whole game; every round the grind turns it one full turn and the whole machine with it. The only piece in the game with an arm, and the only piece whose position is permanent.

components.name: grain_pellet
components.desc: Score piece: 15mm-diameter, 5mm-thick domed washer with a 9mm hole, smooth and untoothed so it can never be confused with a gear. Threads onto a sack_spindle rod; a stack's height is the score, readable across the table. The shared granary holds all 28 and drains as grinds pay out — the game's clock.

components.name: sack_spindle
components.desc: Score post: 40mm round base, 1mm chevron texture on its skirt, with a 8.5mm rod standing 62mm tall — capacity 12 grain_pellet with room to lift the top one off with a thumbnail.

components.name: granary_bin
components.desc: Open bin, ~70 x 50 x 25mm, thumb scallop cut into one long wall, 1mm chevron relief on the front. Holds the grain_pellet supply within reach of every seat; as it empties the table can see the race running down.

setup.text: Set the yard_board in the middle of the table with all 37 pins empty. The 18 outer pins are ringed with a raised sill: those are the YARD PINS, the only pins a millstone or the fixed crank may ever stand on. The other 19 pins take supply gears only.

Put the whole gear supply in an open pile beside the board where every seat can reach it: 14 gear_low, 7 gear_high, 3 gear_tandem. Anyone may take from it on their turn, and what is left in the pile is part of the game's clock.

Fill the granary_bin with all 28 grain_pellet and set it beside the board. This shared granary is the other part of the clock: every grind draws from it, and the moment it is empty the milling stops for good.

Each player takes one millstone — the hub prisms have three, four, five and six flats, and the one you take is your mark for the whole game — and one sack_spindle, which stands in front of their seat, empty.

Choose a first player any way you like; they are the start player of round one and play passes clockwise. The first player stands the crank_gear on any empty yard pin. THE CRANK IS THEN FIXED FOR THE WHOLE GAME: no rule ever moves it again, and every grind for the rest of the game turns the machine out from this one pin. This makes the runner's job simple and permanent — the power never relocates, so a long chain built to it stays built to it.

Now seat the millstones in a snake so that the seats that must wait are not punished for seeing the power. Starting with the LAST player and moving clockwise to the FIRST player, each in turn stands their millstone on any still-empty yard pin. A millstone is not fixed — a player may later SHIFT it on their turn — but it stays where it is until they spend a whole turn to move it. Setup is bind-tested like everywhere else: give the crank a quarter turn once every piece is down, and it will turn — the eighteen yard pins form one ring with the inner pins still empty, so at most four millstones and a crank standing on an eighteen-pin ring cannot close a loop of any length at all.

turn.text: MESHING (the fact the whole game runs on). Two pieces on neighbouring pins mesh only if their teeth are at the same height: a gear_low meshes with a gear_low, a gear_high with a gear_high, and a low never touches a high. A gear_tandem, a millstone and the crank_gear all carry teeth over the full height, so they mesh with anything on a neighbouring pin. Pins that are not neighbours never mesh, whatever stands on them.

THE FIXED CRANK. The crank_gear stands exactly where setup put it; no player may lift it, no rule moves it, and it cannot be blocked off because nothing ever sits between pins except standing pieces. It is the single permanent source of power, and everything driven by it must lead back here through meshed teeth. Because it cannot move, a chain built to it is not a trap that the start player can next round make pointless by walking the power away — the power is where it was, and your chain to it is worth more the longer it is.
ACTIONS. Each round, beginning with the start player and going clockwise, every player takes exactly one action: PLACE, SHIFT or PASS.

PLACE. Take one gear of any kind from the supply — gear_low, gear_high or gear_tandem — and stand it on any empty pin, yard pin or inner. Then test it, below. This is the whole game's engine: every gear you set down either lengthens your own drive (more grist each grind), welds a bridge across a tooth tier where your drive was stuck, or — placed on the right pin — flips a neighbour's drive dead, below in DIRECTION.

SHIFT. Instead of placing, lift your own millstone off its pin and stand it on any other empty yard pin. You may not put it back where it came from. Then test it, below. Shifting costs a whole turn, and a shifted millstone starts its new life at whatever parity the floor offers, so it is a reposition away from a flipped-dead seat — not a way to gain grist for free.

TEST FOR A BIND. Every single time a piece arrives on a pin — a PLACE or a SHIFT — you test it there and then: turn the crank_gear a quarter turn by its knob, and nudge one gear in every separate cluster the crank cannot reach. If anything refuses to move, you have closed a loop containing an odd number of meshes and the yard is BOUND — an odd ring of gears physically cannot turn. A binding PLACE or SHIFT is still a move you may attempt, and it is offered exactly like every other move: you try it, and if it binds the piece comes straight back off and nothing is left standing, because adding more gears can never free a bound yard. The attempt costs your action — the placed gear returns to the supply, the shifted millstone returns to the pin it left, your turn ends with nothing done, and no pellet is ever paid or drained for it. So there is no ambiguity, and no reading to guess: a binding placement is a legal move that is offered to you and resolved by spending your turn on it; it is never simply withheld from the list of moves you may choose.

PASS. Do nothing this round. A player with no legal action must pass. Passing does nothing to the machine, nothing to the supply and nothing to the granary, which is why it is almost never right: while you pass, everyone else's grinds drain the shared granary toward an end you are not building toward. Passing never ends the milling on its own and never wins it — passing merely spends the round, exactly like a binding placement that reverted.

THE GRIND. When everyone has acted, the start player turns the crank_gear one full turn clockwise, the way the arrow on its cap points, and everybody watches the millstones. The crank always turns at this point: every move that could have bound the yard was tested as it was made and taken straight back if it bound. If it somehow will not turn, a test was missed — undo this round's moves one at a time in reverse order (placed gears back to the supply, shifted millstones back to the pins they left) until the crank turns again, then grind from there. For each millstone, walk the running chain back to the crank and count the gears on the SHORTEST route (recount every grind — the machine changes as gears are added). A millstone grinds a number of grain_pellet equal to that count if and only if it turns clockwise (odd count) — a millstone that turns counterclockwise, or cannot reach the crank at all, grinds nothing. Pay every pellet that is owed from the granary_bin, threaded onto its owner's sack_spindle.

DIRECTION (the other fact, and the saboteur's weapon). Meshed gears turn opposite ways, so a millstone grinds clockwise exactly when an ODD number of gears stands between it and the crank along its shortest running chain, and turns backwards — dead — when that count is even. A millstone meshing straight into the crank (zero gears) is therefore dead. Now the attack: place one gear so it becomes the new shortest route into a neighbour's mill and you flip that count by one, turning a grinding millstone dead; place it so it flips a dead one alive. And because a longer chain pays more grist per grind, the same fact makes every drive a temptation — a mill deep in its own long machine amasses grist fast, but stands one good gear away from being deadened. Nobody has to count parity: turn the crank and look at which way each millstone turns.

A SHORT GRANARY. If the granary_bin does not hold enough grain_pellet to pay everything this grind owes, the payout is not skipped and it is not rounded: hand the remaining pellets out one at a time, beginning with the start player and going clockwise, to each owner still owed something, going round again if anyone is still owed, until either every debt is paid or the bin is empty. Any debt the empty bin cannot cover is simply never paid, and the game ends at the end of this round.
Pass the start player role one seat clockwise (the crank still does not move) and begin the next round.

end.text: The game ends at the end of the round in which the last gear leaves the supply pile, and also at the end of any round in which the granary_bin is emptied — whether that grind paid every mill in full or ran the bin dry part-way through under A SHORT GRANARY. Whichever comes first, that round's grind is played out in full before the game stops. A single pass on its own never reaches the end, because one player passing draws nothing from the supply and nothing from the granary: the end is only ever earned by building and grinding, so there is no way to slip past a slower neighbour by stalling alone — you just let them drain the granary and win the race you refused to run. (Only a whole round that seizes — every seat inert — skims the granary, under A STALLED MILL below.)

A STALLED MILL (the clock that cannot be stalled). At the end of any round in which the machine did not change and nothing ground — no gear successfully placed (one that came to rest on a pin), no millstone successfully shifted to a new pin, and the grind paid no pellet at all — the mill has seized for that round and pays a maintenance toll of one grain_pellet from the granary_bin, discarded to no one. If that toll empties the granary_bin, the game ends under the first condition above; otherwise the round is simply over and play continues from the next round. A round counts as having changed the machine if any gear ended it on a pin it had not stood on or any millstone ended it on a pin it had not stood on, even if nothing was paid; a round that empties the granary is already over, above. This is what guarantees a game always ends: you cannot run the clock out by passing or by attempting binding moves that revert, because a whole round that does nothing drains one pellet from the granary toward the end rather than parking the machine. And because a seized round only skims the granary instead of stopping the milling, it never hands the win to whoever happened to be ahead when the machine seized — the grind goes on until a real end is earned.

win.text: Compare sack_spindles: the tallest stack of grain_pellet wins, and it is tall enough to judge from across the table without counting. If two or more stacks are level, the win goes to the tied player whose millstone turned clockwise on the final grind; if that still does not separate them, they share the win.
